title: Group 7 - The Halogens
content:
# Group 7 - The Halogens

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the properties of Group 7 elements
- Explain the trend in reactivity down the group
- Describe displacement reactions of halogens
- Compare halogens with alkali metals in terms of trends

## Introduction

The **halogens** (Group 7) are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, and astatine. They are reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂). Unlike Group 1, reactivity **decreases** down the group.

## Key Concepts

### Group 7 Elements

| Element | Symbol | Atomic number | Configuration | State at room temp | Colour |
|---------|--------|---------------|---------------|-------------------|--------|
| Fluorine | F | 9 | 2,7 | Gas | Pale yellow |
| Chlorine | Cl | 17 | 2,8,7 | Gas | Green-yellow |
| Bromine | Br | 35 | 2,8,18,7 | Liquid | Red-brown |
| Iodine | I | 53 | 2,8,18,18,7 | Solid | Grey-black (purple vapour) |

### Physical Properties

**Trends going down the group:**

| Property | Trend | Reason |
|----------|-------|--------|
| Melting/boiling point | Increases | Larger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces |
| State | Gas → Liquid → Solid | Stronger forces |
| Colour | Darker | More electrons, different light absorption |
| Atomic radius | Increases | More electron shells |
| Reactivity | Decreases | Harder to gain electron |

**All halogens:**
- Exist as diatomic molecules (X₂)
- Are non-metals
- Are poor conductors
- Have low melting/boiling points (molecular)
- Are toxic/harmful

### Why Are They Reactive?

**All Group 7 elements:**
- Have **7 electrons** in their outer shell
- Need to **gain 1 electron** to achieve stable octet
- Form **-1 ions** (halide ions: F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻)

$$\text{Cl} + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^-$$

### Why Does Reactivity Decrease Down the Group?

- Atoms get larger down the group
- Outer shell is further from nucleus
- More shielding from inner electrons
- Less attraction for incoming electron
- Harder to gain the electron needed
- Reaction is slower and less vigorous

**Compare with Group 1:**
- Group 1: Reactivity **increases** down (easier to LOSE electron)
- Group 7: Reactivity **decreases** down (harder to GAIN electron)

### Displacement Reactions

**Rule:** A more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive halogen from its compounds.

**Testing this:**
Add halogen solution to solutions of halide salts:

| | + NaCl | + NaBr | + NaI |
|---------|--------|--------|-------|
| Cl₂(aq) | No reaction | ✓ Orange (Br₂) | ✓ Brown (I₂) |
| Br₂(aq) | No reaction | No reaction | ✓ Brown (I₂) |
| I₂(aq) | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction |

**Equations:**
$$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{2NaBr} \rightarrow \text{2NaCl} + \text{Br}_2$$
$$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{2NaI} \rightarrow \text{2NaCl} + \text{I}_2$$
$$\text{Br}_2 + \text{2NaI} \rightarrow \text{2NaBr} + \text{I}_2$$

**Ionic equations:**
$$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{2Br}^- \rightarrow \text{2Cl}^- + \text{Br}_2$$

### Reactions with Metals

**Halogens react with metals to form halides:**

$$\text{2Na} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{2NaCl}$$
$$\text{2Fe} + \text{3Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{2FeCl}_3$$
$$\text{2Fe} + \text{3Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{2FeBr}_3$$

**Observations:**
- Vigorous reaction
- White/coloured smoke (metal halide)
- Heat released (exothermic)

### Reactions with Hydrogen

$$\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{2HCl}$$
$$\text{H}_2 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{2HBr}$$

**Reactivity with hydrogen:**
- Fluorine: Explosive in dark
- Chlorine: Explosive in sunlight
- Bromine: Needs heating
- Iodine: Needs strong heating, reversible

### Uses of Halogens

| Halogen | Uses |
|---------|------|
| Fluorine | Toothpaste (fluoride), Teflon |
| Chlorine | Water purification, bleach, PVC |
| Bromine | Flame retardants, pesticides |
| Iodine | Antiseptic, photography, thyroid |

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Explain why chlorine is more reactive than bromine.

**Solution:**
- Chlorine has fewer electron shells than bromine
- The outer shell of chlorine is closer to the nucleus
- There is less shielding from inner electrons in chlorine
- The nucleus has a stronger attraction for incoming electrons
- Chlorine gains an electron more easily than bromine
- Therefore, chlorine is more reactive

---

**Example 2:** Predict and explain what happens when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution.

**Solution:**
**Prediction:**
- A reaction will occur
- Bromine is more reactive than iodine
- Bromine will displace iodine

**Observations:**
- The orange/yellow bromine colour disappears
- The solution turns brown (iodine is released)

**Equation:**
$$\text{Br}_2 + \text{2KI} \rightarrow \text{2KBr} + \text{I}_2$$

---

**Example 3:** Explain why iodine cannot displace bromine from sodium bromide solution.

**Solution:**
- Iodine is less reactive than bromine
- A less reactive halogen cannot displace a more reactive one
- Iodine is larger, with outer electrons further from nucleus
- Iodine has more shielding
- Iodine is less able to attract/gain electrons than bromine
- No reaction occurs

---

**Example 4:** Compare the trends in reactivity for Group 1 and Group 7.

**Solution:**

| | Group 1 | Group 7 |
|---|---------|----------|
| Reactivity trend | Increases down | Decreases down |
| Reason | Easier to LOSE electron | Harder to GAIN electron |
| Most reactive | Caesium (bottom) | Fluorine (top) |
| Least reactive | Lithium (top) | Iodine (bottom) |

Both trends are explained by atomic size and shielding, but the effect is opposite because one group loses electrons and the other gains them.

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Thinking reactivity increases down Group 7 (like Group 1)
- **Correct:** Reactivity DECREASES down Group 7

- **Mistake:** Writing Cl instead of Cl₂ for chlorine
- **Correct:** Halogens exist as diatomic molecules: Cl₂, Br₂, I₂

- **Mistake:** Thinking any halogen can displace any other
- **Correct:** Only MORE reactive halogens displace LESS reactive ones

## Practice Questions

1. State the colour and state at room temperature of:
   a) Chlorine (1 mark)
   b) Bromine (1 mark)
   c) Iodine (1 mark)

2. Describe and explain the trend in reactivity of halogens going down Group 7. (4 marks)

3. Predict what happens when:
   a) Chlorine is bubbled through potassium bromide solution (2 marks)
   b) Iodine is added to sodium chloride solution (2 marks)
   Write equations where reactions occur.

4. Compare the reactivity trends in Group 1 and Group 7. Explain why they are opposite. (4 marks)

5. Write a balanced equation for the reaction of chlorine with iron. (2 marks)

6. Why do halogens have low melting and boiling points compared to metals? (2 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Halogens | Group 7 elements (F, Cl, Br, I, At) |
| Diatomic | Existing as molecules of two atoms (e.g., Cl₂) |
| Halide | A negative ion formed from a halogen (e.g., Cl⁻) |
| Displacement | When a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one |

## Summary

- **Group 7** = Halogens: F, Cl, Br, I, At
- Exist as **diatomic molecules** (X₂)
- **7 outer electrons** → gain 1 to form X⁻ ions
- **Reactivity decreases down the group** (harder to gain electron)
- Going down: **Gases → Liquid → Solid**, colours get darker
- **Displacement:** More reactive halogen displaces less reactive
- Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻; Br₂ displaces I⁻; I₂ displaces nothing
- **Opposite trend to Group 1** (losing vs gaining electrons)
